content: Tucatinib increases the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Close monitoring is recommended. Tucatinib also affects hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism, further increasing the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. Concomitant use with CYP3A substrates should be avoided, as even minimal changes in drug concentration can lead to severe or life-threatening toxicities. If co-administration is unavoidable, the dose of the CYP3A substrate should be reduced according to its product labeling, and close monitoring is essential. Ulipristal increases the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution and close monitoring are advised. Patients should be monitored for adverse effects of BCRP substrates, and their doses should be adjusted as per product labeling. Vandetanib increases the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter and reducing metabolism. Caution is advised when co-administering glecaprevir/pibrentasvir with BCRP inhibitors, and close monitoring is necessary. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir also increases the levels or effects of velpatasvir through other mechanisms, likely by increasing plasma concentrations of P-gp and BCRP substrates. Close monitoring is required. Vemurafenib increases the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by reducing metabolism. Conversely, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir increases the levels or effects of vemurafenib by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter and reducing metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. Similarly, venetoclax increases the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter, and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir increases venetoclax levels through the same mechanism. Close monitoring is advised. Verapamil increases the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter, and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir increases verapamil levels through the same mechanism. Close monitoring is necessary. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir also increases the levels or effects of vinblastine and vincristine via the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Voclosporin, an OATP1B1 inhibitor, may increase the concentration of OATP1B1 substrates, including glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. While the clinical significance is unclear, monitoring for adverse reactions of OATP1B1 substrates is advised when co-administered with voclosporin. Voriconazole increases the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir increases the levels or effects of voxilaprevir via the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. Alternative drugs should be considered, as co-administration is not recommended. Pruritus (7%) and skin or subcutaneous tissue disorders, such as angioedema, have been reported. Hepatobiliary disorders, including hepatic decompensation and failure, have occurred, particularly in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B or C) or a history of prior hepatic decompensation. Co-administration with atazanavir or rifampin is contraindicated. Hepatitis B virus reactivation may occur in patients co-infected with HCV and HBV. Postmarketing cases of hepatic decompensation or failure, including fatal outcomes, have been reported. No dosage adjustment is required for people who inject drugs (PWID) or those on medication-assisted treatment (MAT) for opioid use disorder, as safety and efficacy are similar to those without a history of injection drug use. There is insufficient human data to determine the risk of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir on pregnancy outcomes. It is unknown if the drug is distributed in human breast milk. In lactating rodents, glecaprevir and pibrentasvir were present in milk without observed effects on the growth and development of nursing pups. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the drug and potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant. Glecaprevir is metabolized by CYP3A4 (secondary), with a half-life of 6 hours, while pibrentasvir has a half-life of 13 hours. Oral pellets should be sprinkled on a small amount of soft food with low water content (e.g., peanut butter, chocolate hazelnut spread, cream cheese, thick jam, or Greek yogurt) that adheres to a spoon and can be swallowed without chewing. Liquids or foods that may cause the drug to dissolve quickly should be avoided, as this may reduce its effectiveness. Tablets should be taken with food at the same time once daily. Both tablets and pellets should be stored at or below 30°C (86°F).
